title: What is the difference between Kafka Connect and writing your own producer/consumer — Connect is config-only (no code), handles scaling/fault-tolerance/offset-tracking automatically, has 100+ pre-built connectors (JDBC, S3, Elasticsearch, MongoDB, Debezium CDC) — you write a producer/consumer only when Connect does not fit your use case?
shortTitle: What is the difference between Kafka Connect and writing your own producer/consumer?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka Connect and a hand-written producer or consumer are two ways to move data to or from Kafka, with a clear trade-off. Connect is configuration-only, so for standard integrations you write no code; the runtime handles scaling by splitting work into tasks across workers, fault tolerance by restarting failed tasks, and offset tracking automatically, and it ships with a large catalogue of pre-built connectors for systems like JDBC databases, S3, Elasticsearch, MongoDB, and change-data-capture via Debezium. A custom producer or consumer is code you own that gives you full control and arbitrary logic, which you choose only when no connector fits, when you need bespoke business processing, or when the integration is unusual.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, Kafka Connect is like using a standard, pre-approved courier contract: you tick a box for which building and what to carry, and the courier company handles trucks, backups, and remembering the last delivery, with no effort from you. Writing your own producer or consumer is like hiring and training your own private driver: far more work and ongoing maintenance, but the only option when you need them to do something unusual that the standard contract does not cover, like inspecting each parcel and making a decision on the spot.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use Kafka Connect for standard, config-only data movement with built-in scaling and offset handling, and write your own producer or consumer only when you need custom logic that no connector provides.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka Connect and a hand-written producer or consumer are two ways to move data to or from Kafka, with a clear trade-off. Connect is configuration-only, so for standard integrations you write no code; the runtime handles scaling by splitting work into tasks across workers, fault tolerance by restarting failed tasks, and offset tracking automatically, and it ships with a large catalogue of pre-built connectors for systems like JDBC databases, S3, Elasticsearch, MongoDB, and change-data-capture via Debezium. A custom producer or consumer is code you own that gives you full control and arbitrary logic, which you choose only when no connector fits, when you need bespoke business processing, or when the integration is unusual.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, Kafka Connect is like using a standard, pre-approved courier contract: you tick a box for which building and what to carry, and the courier company handles trucks, backups, and remembering the last delivery, with no effort from you. Writing your own producer or consumer is like hiring and training your own private driver: far more work and ongoing maintenance, but the only option when you need them to do something unusual that the standard contract does not cover, like inspecting each parcel and making a decision on the spot.

**One line to remember:** Use Kafka Connect for standard, config-only data movement with built-in scaling and offset handling, and write your own producer or consumer only when you need custom logic that no connector provides.

sections.s2_technical:
With a hand-written integration you own the entire lifecycle. For a producer you configure a client, build records, call send, handle the futures, deal with retries and errors, and decide batching and acks. For a consumer you write the poll loop, deserialize, process, commit offsets, handle rebalances, and manage threading and shutdown. You also build operational concerns yourself: how to scale across instances, how to restart cleanly, how to track and recover position, and how to monitor. This is the right level of effort when your logic is genuinely bespoke, but it is a lot of repetitive, error-prone plumbing for a standard copy from a database into Kafka.

Kafka Connect removes that plumbing for common cases. You submit a JSON configuration naming a connector class and its parameters, and the runtime runs it. It handles scaling by dividing the work into tasks and spreading them across worker nodes, so a JDBC source with many tables or an S3 sink with many partitions runs in parallel without you writing a thread pool. It handles fault tolerance by detecting a failed task or worker and restarting the task elsewhere. And it handles offset tracking automatically, storing source offsets in an internal topic and managing sink consumer offsets, so restarts resume correctly without you writing commit logic.

The connector ecosystem is a major practical advantage. There are many pre-built, tested connectors for databases, object storage, search engines, document stores, and change-data-capture, so an integration that would take days to write and harden as a custom consumer is often a single configuration file that is already battle-tested in production elsewhere. Connect also supports lightweight transformation through single-message transforms for small reshaping, and pluggable converters for the wire format, so JSON, Avro, or Protobuf are a configuration choice rather than code.

The decision rule is about fit. You choose Connect when a suitable connector exists, the transformation needed is light, and you want operational concerns handled for you, which is the majority of integrate-with-an-external-system cases. You write your own producer or consumer when no connector fits the system or protocol, when you need rich, stateful, or conditional business logic as the data moves, when the processing is really an application rather than a copy, or when you want tight control over semantics that a connector does not expose. The senior nuances are that you can still deploy Connect in distributed mode for production resilience while running custom apps alongside it; that a common anti-pattern is reinventing a JDBC source as a brittle custom poller when a connector already exists; that Connect's at-least-once default means sink idempotency still matters; and that heavy enrichment or joins belong in a stream-processing application, with Connect handling the ingest and egress at the edges.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem at National Bank of India is that the team kept hand-writing consumers for every integration, and the maintenance burden and bugs were piling up, yet some cases genuinely needed custom code.

Problem 1 — a developer wrote a custom consumer that polled the transactions table and published to Kafka, including hand-rolled offset tracking in a side table, and it repeatedly broke on restarts and lost its place. This is exactly what a JDBC Source Connector would have replaced with a configuration file that tracks offsets reliably and scales automatically.

Problem 2 — archiving a topic to cloud storage was another bespoke consumer that nobody wanted to maintain, duplicating file-writing and offset-commit logic. This is exactly what an S3 Sink Connector replaces.

Problem 3 — one case genuinely needed custom code: enriching each transaction with a live fraud score from an internal service and branching on the result, which no connector can do. This is exactly where a hand-written consumer is correct.

The code will model a `ConnectPipeline` that moves table rows to a topic and the topic to storage purely by configuration, and a `CustomConsumer` that does bespoke per-record enrichment and branching, so the demo contrasts the two approaches side by side. The demo step is: run the Connect-style source and sink with zero business logic, then run the custom consumer that scores and branches each transaction, and observe which concerns each approach handles.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    id         BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO transactions (id, account_id, amount) VALUES
    (1, 'SAV2001', 20000.00),
    (2, 'CUR3001', 750000.00);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# connectors/txn-jdbc-source.json  (Connect = config only, no code)
# { "name":"txn-source",
#   "config":{ "connector.class":"io.confluent.connect.jdbc.JdbcSourceConnector",
#              "connection.url":"jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/bankdb",
#              "table.whitelist":"transactions","mode":"incrementing",
#              "incrementing.column.name":"id","topic.prefix":"bank." } }

# application.yml (only the CUSTOM consumer needs app config)
spring:
  kafka:
    consumer:
      group-id: fraud-enrichment
bank:
  fraud:
    threshold: 500000
```

```bash

javac com/bank/integration/demo/ConnectVsCustomDemo.java
java com.bank.integration.demo.ConnectVsCustomDemo

# Connect path in reality: submit config, no app to deploy
curl -X POST http://localhost:8083/connectors -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d @connectors/txn-jdbc-source.json

# Custom path in reality: build and deploy an app
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/integration-choice-service-1.0.0.jar
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a transactions table with a small transaction for Rajesh and a large one for Priya, processed by both approaches.

Step 1: In the Connect style, the source connector copies both rows into a topic. It does not inspect or transform them; it just moves them, and the runtime tracks the offset so a restart resumes correctly. No business code exists in this path.

Step 2: The sink connector copies the topic records out to cloud storage, again as a pure copy, with the runtime committing offsets after the write. The entire pipeline was two configuration files.

Step 3: In the custom style, the hand-written consumer reads the first transaction for Rajesh. It calls an internal fraud-scoring service to enrich the record, gets a low score, and because the amount is small it branches to pass. This per-record enrichment and branching is logic no connector can express.

Step 4: The consumer reads Priya's large transaction, enriches it with a high score, and because the amount exceeds the threshold it branches to hold the transaction for review.

Step 5: The contrast is clear: the Connect path moved data with zero code but no decision-making, while the custom path required code precisely because it makes per-record decisions.

Step 6: The output shows the config-only import and archive, then the custom consumer passing the small transaction and holding the large one.

```
2026-10-24 23:34:12 [INFO] === KAFKA CONNECT style: config only, no business logic ===
2026-10-24 23:34:12 [INFO] connect-source imported id=1 (runtime tracks offset)
2026-10-24 23:34:12 [INFO] connect-source imported id=2 (runtime tracks offset)
2026-10-24 23:34:12 [INFO] connect-sink archived 2 records to S3 (no code)
2026-10-24 23:34:12 [INFO] === CUSTOM CONSUMER style: needed for per-record enrichment + branching ===
2026-10-24 23:34:12 [INFO] custom: PASS txn id=1 account=SAV2001 score=10
2026-10-24 23:34:12 [WARNING] custom: HOLD txn id=2 account=CUR3001 amount=Rs.750000 score=90
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka Connect and a hand-written producer or consumer are two ways to move data to and from Kafka, and the difference is a clear trade-off between configuration and control. Connect is configuration-only: for standard integrations I write no code, and the runtime handles scaling by splitting the work into tasks across workers, fault tolerance by restarting failed tasks on healthy workers, and offset tracking automatically so restarts resume cleanly. It also ships with a large catalogue of pre-built, battle-tested connectors for databases, object storage, search engines, document stores, and change-data-capture, so an integration that would take days to harden as a custom consumer is often a single configuration file.

A custom producer or consumer is code I own, which means I handle the client, the poll loop, deserialization, offset commits, rebalances, threading, retries, and monitoring myself. That is a lot of repetitive plumbing, but it is exactly the right level when the logic is genuinely bespoke, when no connector fits the system or protocol, or when the processing is really an application that enriches, joins, or branches on each record rather than a straight copy.

The decision rule I apply is about fit. If a suitable connector exists and the transformation needed is light, I use Connect and let it handle the operational concerns, optionally using single-message transforms for small reshaping and choosing the wire format through a converter. If I need rich, stateful, or conditional business logic, I write my own consumer.

At National Bank of India I lived both sides of this. We had a custom consumer that polled the transactions table with hand-rolled offset tracking that kept losing its place on restarts, and replacing it with a JDBC source connector made the problem disappear because Connect tracks offsets for me and scales automatically; archiving a topic to cloud storage became an S3 sink connector instead of another bespoke consumer. But enriching each transaction with a live fraud score and branching on the result stayed as a hand-written consumer, because that per-record decision is logic no connector can express. The senior nuances I add are that heavy enrichment or joins belong in a stream-processing application with Connect handling ingest and egress at the edges, that reinventing a JDBC source as a brittle custom poller is a common anti-pattern, and that Connect being at-least-once by default means sink idempotency still matters.

Idempotent producer: prevents duplicate messages on retry
